utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The late start is also due to some technical problems. So if our technicians are moving around the courtroom, you know why it is. Good morning to you, Mr. Novakovic. I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Misetic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to follow up on a point where we left off last week. I had asked about a unit known as the Mindjusari, which translated is "the ear-ring wearers" or "the ear-ring unit." You advised me that the Mindjusari were a band. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that they were a music band.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was there a military unit in the RSK known as the Mindjusari?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to now call up 1D61-0373, please. It is a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, before we start that clip, do you recognise that individual, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, on the morning of the 4th of August, Mr. Radic was up on the Dinara defending RSK positions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And he was a commander of a unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. He was a coordinator. He was the Chief of Staff of the Corps at the time. In other words, he wasn't a commander of a unit; rather, he coordinated the activities of several units the along that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which units he was coordinating?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. There was the 1st Light Poljice Brigade there, and some others from reinforcements from the staff, several other brigades, but I don't know which elements were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: MUP forces as well, police forces?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is possible that there was one unit of the special forces of the MUP. They had a small units, some 100 men strong, roughly. I do believe that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could play the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Lieutenant-Colonel, do you possibly have a message for the citizens? "Well, they should be as happy as I am. There is no need for panic or worry. Those that are over there doing their tasks should be doing them properly. Women should be happy and not crying. There are no problems. We shall return successfully. Cheers. "No problem. There is no problem. We will return successfully. Cheers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic. On the French channel, I hear B/C/S, and the French interpreters informed us on the French channel that they did not receive a transcript of this. There must be then perhaps a mistake, so could we verify, because you know that translating videos comes down often to one of the interpreters following what is said, whether that appears on paper, and the other one then translating from paper, because it almost impossible to follow the speed of speech. So it is a kind of a very sensitive exercise, and, therefore, I would like to verify whether the transcripts are now available or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honour, they were e-mailed at 8.33 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that one misses that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We don't have them at this time in the English booth, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English booth doesn't have them. I heard the same on channel 5 from the French booth. So I suggest that hard copies are prepared and that perhaps we play it at a later stage, 10, 15, 30 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we ply it without the sound right now, just so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can play it without the sound, of course I have no idea of what the evidentiary value of the sound is, but then we should play it without any sound at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I'm move on, Your Honour. I will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could then shift to a different document, 1D61-0361. We'll show this via Sanction in English, and provide a hard copy to the witness in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, there is a report from the 2nd of August from the Ministry of Interior of the so-called RSK, special units administration. It says: "Report on the employment of the police forces at the Dinara." It talks about what forces are in the Dinara under Colonel Radic. That is the individual we just saw on the video. Is that correct, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the third point, the third unit is special unit Dalmatia with the platoon Mindjusari. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection as to what the -- what unit the Mindjusari were and to whom they belonged?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. You've just asked me whether there was a unit called Mindjusari in the Serbia army. I said that I wasn't aware of that. From here, it transpires that it was a platoon. So it could have been some 10 to 15 men who made the unit who were members of the MUP, because in the letterhead, it says that -- or, rather, it was addressed to the Ministry of Interior; and in the letterhead, it says Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where were the Mindjusari quartered in Knin?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of them being quartered there. I don't have much information relating to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D941, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D941 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, I think the registrar printed out the transcript that was sent this morning, and they have been provided to the booth. So all the booths now have at least a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. If we could play the video then, please, from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Journalist: Lieutenant-Colonel, do you possibly have a message for the citizens? "Radic: Well, they should be as happy as I am. There is no need for panic or worry. Those that are over there doing their tasks should be doing them probably. Women should be happy and not crying. There are no problems. We shall return successfully. Cheers. "Unidentified Male: There are no problems we should return successfully. Cheers. "Unidentified Male: Many regards to our dear citizens from the Mindjusari who have come here to assist -- we have come here to assist our comrades who are in combat here above us. "They need not worry. "Mile: Do not worry. This shall not fall. In the name of the all the Mindjusari, I send regards to all the girls in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. "What about the Ustashas? "Well, as for Ustashas, we say hi to them as well. The outcome is well known. "My regard is via target sight. "Ljute, how do you comment this situation? "Ljute: On behalf of the platoon of the Mindjusari, the Knin volunteers, and combatants, my message is that our co-citizens should not panic, that everything shall be okay, and that they should have faith in our army, especially in the police, the milicija."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is there is question coming for the witness first, or is it just from the bar table. The first portion was tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My questions were -- I was out of sequence because of the technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have no objection. I was just seeking clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D942 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic, these types of videos, would you agree with me that they were made in order to have a certain psychological effect in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it possible. It does seem more like an advertisement to me than a combat unit. Evidently these men were not in their units all the time. Judging but the way they look, I'd is that they were only temporarily and they were, for the most part, the music band. As I said, it does look like more a video-clip or a music promotion clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is it about the way they look that leads you to believe that they were not a unit?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying that they were not a unit, but I'm saying they were not a permanent unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what is it about the way how they look that leads you to believe that they were not a permanent unit?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could deduce from their conduct as a whole - that was precisely your question - that they were more concerned about the whole psychological effect than combat; whereas, they should have been there solely for the purposes of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you have been involved - you were an officer in charge of information - would you have been involved in preparing these types of spots for broadcast in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no need for such footage. I should have said that initially, perhaps. Our men were not manning combat positions for the purposes of producing footage. What we were mentioning before, the order on the strict judgement, so this was something that they would do of their own accord. We had no use for that. Our men knew why they were manning combat positions. From 1991 onwards, we did have any such problems. My team or my sector did not involve in such activities in that sort of incentive. Let me not try and engage in propaganda here. We knew why we had to defend our positions. There was no need for such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have on the screen 1D61-0344, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I'm going to show you the 1988 regulations of the Yugoslav national army on the application of the international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY. This is an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It talks about the concept of a military facility in number 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please, in the B/C/S. Oh, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It gives a definition of a military facility. Then if we go to the footnotes there of what was defined as a military facility, number 1 says: "Regular armed forces or other armed formations established for the purpose of participating in hostilities, including also their auxiliary and supplementary parts, as well as persons who, although not members of these forces or formations, actively participate in war operations ..." Point 3: "Equipment, facilities, or other installations of a military nature (barracks, fortifications, ministries of national defence or armed forces, or other military commands and establishments)." 4 includes quart master stores, stores of arms, ammunitions, and material. 6, traffic routes and facilities of military significance, railway tracks, roads, canals, et cetera. 7, equipment and installations of radio and television stations and telephone and telegraph centres of military importance. Now, you, as a trained officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, you agree with me that that is what you learned to be the definition of a military facility, correct, amongst these other definitions included here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, the definition was in paragraph 71. The footnote Mr. Misetic just read says the following may be considered, not just facilities. I think the question should be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- misrepresented what was in the footnote. I had that on my mind as well, because you said that the footnotes there of what was it fined as a military facility; whereas, the footnote says that certain objects or even persons described there may be considered military facilities. So it depends apparently on other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we may have an issue there, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we may have an issue there on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least in presenting it to the witness, you left out "may be." And if that is clear, Mr. Novakovic, Mr. Misetic read to you from a footnote which -- of which the original language says "The following may be considered military facilities," and then Mr. Misetic read a couple of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is there a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I think may be the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is an translation issue, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a different sense that I get from that in the original, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, of course it should be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll verify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you read perhaps the original then, if you have it available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you read the original, then there can be no confusion with the witness; then we might still be confused, but we'll resolve that. Perhaps you read the first line of the footnote of which you quoted certain portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, to be precise, what's listed in the footnote there, it says in the original: [Interpretation] "The following may be considered -- [Previous translation continues] ... [in English] as a JNA officer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You know that I am -- have a degree in political sciences and methodology. The regulations you have shown to me from international law are practically the Geneva Conventions that were implemented in the regulations. Now, the definition itself, as provided in 71, is quite correct. The text in small print is a footnote, and, precisely, as His Honour put it, the following may be considered military facilities. Perhaps somebody was imprecise in using this "may" because a definition has to be very precise. It should use the following formulation. The following shall be considered military facilitates. For instance, a barracks will be considered a military facility if a certain combat unit is billeted there. If there are no combat units billeted at the particular barracks, it will definitely not be a military facility. That's the way I could interpret as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, let's turn to number -- page 33 -- numbered page 33 in the English. This is numbered paragraph 81 in the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 5 of the B/C/S, Mr. Registrar, and if we could scroll over to the left, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This provides a definition of an open city: "A place may be proclaimed an open city even before the inception of hostilities. In order for such place to enjoy full protection as an open city, it is necessary that the other party to the conflict also accords it this status. "Usually, the following conditions are agreed upon ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the right, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... that the place is not defended and that there are no armed forces in it." Let start there, Mr. Novakovic. Knin was defended, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one might say that; however, the closest units were towards Dinara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you also had positions on Bulina Strana as well, behind Knin, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit further from Bulina Strana --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the interpreters did not hear what the witness said. You said a little bit further from Bulina Strana, and then did you add something to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a little bit further on, towards hinterland and the village of Ducic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the second part says there are no armed forces in it. Now, there, in fact, were armed forces of the RSK in Knin on the 4th of August. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very clear that, apart from the command, there were no other forces. If you deem the command forces, then you are right. That was the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about logistics: Mr. Bjelanovic, the Senjak bearings. They were also there on the 4th. Correct.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deemed them to be part of the Main Staff. That's logistics. Just like my information department was part of the Main Staff, so was the logistics. There is no dispute over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, how would you drive the logistics out of the Senjak barracks, let's say? How would you get the logistics out?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knin had only two or three streets, and they only could get out of the town that way. There was only one main street practically and a couple of back streets, and everything could only happen along the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Novakovic, what I'm asking you is, if the order gets passed, let's say, to Mr. Bjelanovic for more logistics to go someplace, were you going to get in the truck and drive it? Was Mr. Bjelanovic going to personally get behind the wheel of the truck and drive it around?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are rules applied to logistics, just like in every other area. Depending on the depot, the whole system is in place and plans according to which this is being done. As you have probably read in my C.V., for a number of years, I was at head of the logistics, and everyone knows that are plans in place. It is not done by the head of the service or the department. You have a whole array of tasks, and a lot of people are involved in carrying out these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say "a lot of people," you mean a lot of soldiers, right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only soldiers, I was referring to all the people working in this chain, but they need not have to be in Knin. It goes from the lowest level unit to -- up to the Main Staff. They were all involved in the process. The depot did not necessarily have to be in Knin, where Mr. Bjelanovic was in charge of quarter masters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read 2, 3, and 4 to you: "The conditions are that military units do not pass through and material is not transported over its territory." Now, the logistics, as you just told us, there were one or two streets in Knin over which the logistics could travel. So if Mr. Bjelanovic wanted to move logistics past the Senjak barracks, he would be passing through the streets of Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I explained that there were only quarter masters assets, and there was no transport on that day. There was no ammunition ever in Knin. But, indeed, there were transport from Senjak, carrying food and clothes, and, of course, they had to pass through that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you wanted to move weapons from some of the tunnels, where some of the weapons had been stored behind Knin towards Stara Straza, and you wanted to move them up to the Dinara, you would have to drive them through Knin, right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, the weapons were not at the place where you mentioned. The weapons were with the units, and there was no need for it to be transported. It was always in the possession of units, and there was no need for the transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The economic and industrial plants in that place stop all activities of military significance or activities for military purposes." 4 is that: "The place discontinue all communication with the national and allied armed forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before we continue, I read this "open city" paragraph, which apparently says that you need an agreement on that and these are the usual conditions. Was there agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, that is my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why go through all what could have been the conditions that could have been, and these are the usual conditions. But if there is no agreement, why spend so much time on conditions that were never negotiated and reached the level of a conclusion, which means that Knin apparently, according to this rule, never obtained the status of an open city. Is it claimed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I think it may be the position of the Prosecution that Knin -- they've used several witnesses to claim it was an undefended town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, we have heard a lot about what there was, as far as military facilities and military units are concerned. But this appears, this rule 81, seems to focus on an agreement and obtaining a formal status of, which until now, I think it is the first time I hear that to be denied, where I never heard it to be claimed. Is that right, Mr. Hedaraly? His body language seems to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree that it wasn't claimed, but I think de facto the Prosecution position is that Knin was an undefended city, and that there were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did not obtain the formal status under rule 81. I mean, apart from what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Because they never sought it, and that is my ultimate point. They never even in the first place even sought that it be declared an open city, or met those conditions, because they weren't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter is clear now, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... asked the witness what he knows about such an agreement, if he knew anything about it. I mean, that seems to make more sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, no, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... to go in to quite a lot of details, because, you see, we come to point 4 soon, which says "The parties to the conflict may agree on other conditions for each individual case." So we have there an endless area to explore, where -- The issue is clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge, if I may, the witnesses come to court to tell a story and to tell, you know, that nothing was happening in Knin, there were no soldiers in Knin, there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. That's all facts --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a JNA document. If that were the case and they want to now claim that Knin shouldn't have been attacked, he knows the regulations or what should have been done to have it declared an open city, or to at least proceed on that path. None of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. There is no claim that it was ever declared an open city, so whether then to go through all of the details, what are the usual conditions, if seems to me -- again, focus on facts, no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I know it wasn't declared an open city, and that is my point, where, on the one hand, it is to eat your cake and to have it, too. It was undefended, we met all the conditions. On the other hand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you made your point very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There is a difference between saying the town is undefended and it's an open city according to regulation. If he doesn't ask him the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we now know that a town can obtain under certain conditions that status. It is not claimed that it ever claimed that status. Therefore, to go into details, we have seen here that some of the elements, factual elements, which may be invoked in the Prosecution's case, could have led perhaps to negotiations and perhaps to endeavoured to have that status claimed. That is clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, if I can take you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I may tender the document into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D943 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have 65 ter 128, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, this is the directive for the use of the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we scroll to the bottom, the date is February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you first tell the Court what is the directive? What is its purpose?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a basic document, and it is at a higher level than an ordinary order. It governs how to use the army and how the defence should be pursued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 of the B/C/S and page 5 in the English please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is a quite extensive document, Mr. Novakovic, and I will not go through all of it with you. However, page 5 discusses the first phase of -- under section 3, which is likely method of aggression and axes of engagement. And if we look at phase one, it says: "This type of aggression is in progress and is being carried out by way of psychological operations." Then it says towards the bottom: "Croatia's likely aim is to exert a strong influence on the population, disorient it, create doubt in the possibility of a defence of the Krajina, and dissatisfaction with its government; to disorganise and divide the state of leadership; to disable an orderly and timely mobilisation of units and the operation development of the army of the SVK; thus creating the conditions for a peaceful reintegration of the RSK. "By achieving or not achieving its aim, through this operation, Croatia would probably create favourable conditions for the reintegration of the RSK into its borders through peaceful or violent means." Mr. Novakovic, as early as February 1995, the army of the SVK was aware that Croatia's first option was to peacefully reintegrate the RSK into Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this is what it says here. There's a difference when you say by peaceful means, or when you put it in inverted commas. It just implies the totally opposite effect. I didn't draft this because I wasn't in charge of that particular job at the time, but, basically, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go do page 8 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just note the record that the inverted commas in the B/C/S does not appear on the English translation as peaceful, as just pointed out by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a 65 ter, so if the Prosecution wants to update the translation and give it us --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think I clarified the record, and that was my only objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If inverted commas do not appear in the translation, then, of course, it is appropriate to have then in, and not just say that it is just for the record. I mean, I do see that it does not appear in the translation, where it does appear in the originals. So, therefore, it should be uploaded in a corrected version. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the top of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it says: (B) is in an aggression with a radical objective. Point 1 is: "Through a maximum use of all state resources, persistent defence and active combat operations, the Serbian army of Krajina in joint actions with parts of the VRS and the VJ shall prevent the capture of territory and defend the integrity of the RSK." Now, that was one of the fundamental principles of the defence of the RSK was that you would be working jointly with parts of the VRS and the VJ. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather say that that was the desire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, didn't you, subsequent to this order, Mr. Novakovic, participate jointly - when I say "you," I mean the SVK with the VRS - in military operations on the Bihac pocket, July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The SVK provided certain support. And as far as its participation is concerned, General Mile Novakovic explained in a number of interviews the role of the Serbian army in the Bihac pocket. The Serbian army of Krajina did not participate directly; rather, it was part of the defence system of Western Bosnia, and there were a couple of officers who were there acting as coordinators. The -- the army of Serbian Krajina did not take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll get into that a little bit later, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 16 in the English, please; subsection 6.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Focus moral and psychological support on creating the conviction among all members of the SVK that the defence of the Serbian cause and the Serbian people in this area is a historic task, and that the unification of the entire Serbian people, which can only be achieved through the struggle of each individual, depends on its realisation." Now, one of your objectives in the ARSK was unification with the Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been a desired and long-term process, but I don't think that was the priority or the primary objective. There was an idea of some sort of unity, and I think that the objective is very chore. We don't need to go into the politics, but their primary goal for the Serbs in Croatia was to have autonomy, and you know what the outcome was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this exhibit and ask that it be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D944, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D944 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, let's go to - it is a video - 1D61-0251.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again an excerpt from that Banja Luka, 7 August programme that you were on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "First of all, the USA, and especially the NATO pact, even when we were -- NATO plans interfered with our aircraft, and they also shelled, as you know, our rockets surrounding Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told we should play it one more time for the -- the translators may not have had the transcript in front of them when we began the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a very short portion, so if it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I heard most of it translated, but I'm not certain that everything was translated. So perhaps we play it again because it was very short.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "First of all, the USA, and especially the NATO pact, even when at one point we were defending ourselves from the HV aviation, NATO plans interfere with our flights or our flight plans, and they also shelled, as you know, our rocket systems surrounding Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, first, where were the rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained from Bulina Strana towards the inland and the village of Padjene. So the surrounding of Knin is a broad area. Actually, that is where the command and the radios were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And did NATO, in fact, attack your rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, we heard this information. I myself am not sure. I suppose that was the case because NATO never refuted, but I cannot claim that with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D945, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D945 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about some facilitates in Knin now. Do you recall -- do you recall telling us, when you were being questioned by Mr. Hedaraly about the nuns convent in Benkovac, you said that the RSK did not make use of religious facilities for military purposes. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was true in principle. Neither the Catholic ones or the Greek orthodox ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you say "in principle." Do you know of specific facilities that violated that principle and that, in fact, were used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to add, in principle and in practice, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know of any exceptions? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to -- Mr. Registrar, if we go to 1D61-0273, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated 25 July 1994. "The conclusion of the ministry of culture and religion is the government has decided that the building of the Catholic monastery should entirely be used for the purposes of the ministry of culture and religion. "Prior to this, it is necessary to relocate the special police unit of the MUP, and to move out the refugees from this building." Now, in fact, special police forces were bordered in the Catholic monastery. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is apparent from this document. I don't think anything about this, but it also mentioned refugees in addition to special police. One should really examine where these refugees had came from, and it is obvious that the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina dealt with this problem and had in mind an intention to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's address that, but, first, before I move on to next piece of evidence. The special police unit there, are you familiar with the fact that the special police unit is the Mindjusari, which is the video we saw at the beginning of this morning sessions, that they were the ones that were headquartered in St. Anthony's Monastery in Knin?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what we have seen, it seems that it could only have been one part of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D946, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D946 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, after this decision was taken, there was then a discussion in the so-called RSK parliament because this decision wasn't implemented, and I would like to show you a clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is 1D61-0239. May we proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. Yes, now I see it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The government has made the decision to place the archive in the monastery, but what do we find there? A special unit. "Mr. Atlagic, I would like to ask you to come with me to chase out this special unit. There is the decision of the government. Mr. Mikelic can show it to you. "All right. Thank you. "Thank you, Mr. Prijic. "Chairmen, representatives of the people. First of all, allow me to say something without trying to be funny, but also not entirely serious. Some of us want to chase out the special unit from the monastery, but more than that, they want to do this to me. But that is the part of the political structures, and that is not entirely impossible, as far as I am concerned. But as far as the special unit is concerned, this wouldn't be such a good option, particularly because, and some keep this as a secret, it was this unit that stopped the Muslim offensive and breach towards Petrovac, and prevented the consolidation of their forces and pushed the Muslims back to where they are right now. "So much ... let's not play public secret. There were some matters that had been referred to in the reports on the government that were being kept secret, but now are publicly dealt with."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, two questions on the video. First, at the end there, he references the fact that this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I haven't asked the question. I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hedaraly has not said anything. He is on his feet, so I'm on alert, and you may continue. That's how I appreciate the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, first, he mentions there that this special unit that is quartered in the monastery fended off the Muslims in the Petrovac area. That's in Bosnia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that activity. I don't know why the minister said this, what his purpose in saying that was. These were parliament debates, and it doesn't necessarily follow that this is true. But I'm not familiar with that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I see what I see. I don't know hear anything. Unless I hear anything, Mr. Misetic will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt, but If I may raise an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may raise an issue. Of course, whether it is appropriate to do it in the presence of the witness, I leave that, because I don't know what you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to seek clarification on the date for the witness, so that he has the actual knowledge of the full video before being asked questions specifically about that meeting. If the question is general like the last one, then there was no objection, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly would be assisted by having a time-frame for the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 10 November 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10 November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that is what it titled in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not seen any titles. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the second question, Mr. Novakovic, regards these discussions in parliament. The discussion in the parliament is that despite the decision of the government from the summer of 1994, the special forces still hadn't move out. Were you familiar with that problem, that the special forces decided not to follow the decision of the government?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to draw your attention to one piece of information. The period we're discussing now is the second half of 1994. I was in the 11th Corps in Vukovar, I wasn't in Knin, so I'm not really familiar with some information dating from that period. I did follow the events but not closely. I was in the detached command of the 11th Corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D947, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D947 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D57, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I'm going to show you the Croatian Ministry of Interior police log-book after the Croatian police took over in Knin, then I'm going show you the entry for the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, this is page 10 in the English and page ten in the B/C/S. If we could scroll to the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's the entry the Zeljko Car. There it is, on the bottom, yes. Now the entry says n 12 August 1995 there was a call into the police. It says: "Discovery of ammunition. He reported around 20 cases of ammunition were found in St. Anthony's monastery." Now, you were in Knin on the 12th of August, Mr. Novakovic. Were you aware of 20 cases of weapons being in St. Anthony's monastery on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you were aware of the discovery of ammunition in St. Anthony's monastery, which was reported on the 12th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. But between the 5th and the 12th of August, all manner of things could happen. Whose weapons they were and how they came to be there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, on the 4th of August, 1995, St. Anthony's monastery was being used by the special police forces of the so-called RSK. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I would pass by that area, and I never saw them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I could have D930, please. This is again Mr. Vrcalj's book. He is the head of artillery of the RSK. And if we could go to page 6 in the English, please, and page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now here is what the artillery officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Page 6, yes, in the B/C/S, mid-page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He talks about the morning of the 4th, and he says -- I'm -- it's numbered page 6 of 25, so if we could scroll to the bottom. Next page in the English, please. He talks about, towards the middle of the page, the 4th of August. And now the head of artillery says: "The most important targets in Knin were the building of the General Staff, the residence of the president, the casern, Severna Kasarna," which is the northern barracks, "the Kasarna Senjak and the main cross-road in Knin?" Do you agree with Mr. Vrcalj that those were the most important targets in Knin?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know in the context in which he used the term "the most important targets." Maybe they were very important in terms -- in political or economic terms. He didn't specify what sort of targets they were. Were they military targets? One could debate about it, but we don't know what the author meant. This was an observation on his part which I need not agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in the English, and it is page 7 at the top in the B/C/S, Mr. Vrcalj, the head of artillery, says in the morning he managed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the top in the English please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Talks about the northern barracks and then says: "I jumped over the fence in the casern and entered the building where I worked up until four months ago." Were you aware that the chief of artillery of the ARSK in the morning of the 4th of August was himself located in the northern barracks?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. The only thing that I know is that he lived in a small bed-sitter ^ in the same building where I lived. I didn't see him on that day or in the following several days. We did not have any professional dealings because our military tasks did not overlap. That's why we wouldn't be in contact that frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, he then says that he went from the northern barracks to the Main Staff building. And he says when he got to the Main Staff -- that the second paragraph, full paragraph in English: "I entered the building and, boy, was there a lot for me to see there. Two shells landed in the parking area between the buildings, exploded, and destroyed the entire car park of the Main Staff. It must have been that one good artillery operator has struck them precisely at that location." Now, do you recall the fact that the car park behind the Main Staff had in fact been hit?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The car park was in fact the yard of the command. There used be to be a volleyball playground. It was an area between the Main Staff and another building. A shell did land there, one shell landed there, inflicting damage onto the vehicles parked there. Of course it -- what one writes depends on one's imagination and on one's intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go down a couple of paragraphs towards the bottom in the English. And it's page 7, last paragraph in the B/C/S. He says: "I asked around about the other commanding officers from the Main Staff since they were not present. There were just a few of us. Some didn't report throughout the day, although their sleeping quarters have been situated in the retirement home which was located some 400 metres away." That is correct, isn't it, that these officers were quartered at the retirement home, who never showed up on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite true. The fact of the matter is that some of the officers were in the old people's home. There was some 40 rooms, whereas 10 to 15 rooms were used by our officers as sleeping quarters. They would go there on their own or in groups and run up to the command. I am not aware of them staying there throughout the day. They were perhaps afraid, but I -- officers, as they were, I don't think that they spent the entire day in the old people's home. This is Vrcalj's personal observation, and I do doubt that this is the way it happened. Some of my associates who had sleeping quarters there did not show up in the morning, not at 5.00 but they showed up at 5.00 at -- at 8.00, and then they stayed there until noon, 12.00, at the very least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could move to page 13 in the English, which is numbered page 12 and page 11 in the B/C/S. That's it. Now -- in the B/C/S, it's the sixth line from the top of the page. It's the second sentence here. This is now talking about what happened after the evacuation order had been issued. Mr. Vrcalj says: "General Bjelanovic made a remark that I had to find the train captain who would pull out the train loaded with ammunition from Stara Straza." Now, were you aware that the railway system in the RSK was being moved to move weapons for the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The passage talks about ammunition, and his question talks about weapons. The second time that happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you were referring to ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ammunition, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, were you aware that the train system was being used to move ammunition?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I observed the fact that Mr. Misetic did not distinguish between that -- weapons and ammunition. I didn't know that at some point - I don't know how many days before the general aggression of the 4th of August, most probably after the 27th of July when Grahovo fell - some of the ammunition from the Golubic depot was transferred by railway in some 13 carriages, I believe, and stored in some of the tunnels. I didn't know exactly which of the tunnel it is was. It could have been the railway leading to Licka Kaldrma, or on the rail track leading to Zadar. But according to what Mr. Vrcalj says, it must have been there at Stara Straza. I only knew that it had been stored away before the 1st of August. But since that was not my business strictly speaking, I did not inquire about it or take part in it. In other words, some of the ammunition was most probably stored in one of the tunnels, and there was some ten to 13 carriages loaded with ammunition. Well, quite probably, there were 13, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I go back, please, to D923.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again General Mrksic's report from the 26th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could go to numbered page 25 in the original, which is page 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, starting at paragraph number 5 at the bottom, General Mrksic reports about the 5th of August in the morning. He says: "Then it was ordered to evacuate 14 railway wagons loaded with ammunition from the tunnel on the axis Stara Straza-Padjene, and to relocate them to Otric-Malovan region, in order to take them to the Republika Srpska Territory." He says: "The train personnel and the security left the wagons during the night, but it would not have been possible to do any constructive since Malovan had already been under the enemy fire." Then he says: "In order to initiate destruction of ammunition in the tunnels near Stara Straza, the armoured train was pushed, in order to insight an explosion due to the inertia and crash with the wagons loaded with ammunition. This operation failed because the train turned over before the entry in the tunnel. It was ordered to blow up the mined ammunition store Golubic, and for that, all preparation had been carried out previously. But due to disruption of communications, it was not possible to forward the order to the store commander." The next pages says: "According to our current knowledge, he tried to activate the ignition system, but an enemy reconnaissance and sabotage group prevented him." Now, were you aware, as someone who was an officer working with General Mrksic, that on the 5th, plan had been activated to try to blow up ammunition depots in both the tunnels at Stara Straza and at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, and I needn't have been. In principle, I don't know that there were any such sabotage activities carried out, nor were there any plans for this. This wasn't the practice applied in our army; although, one could arrive at this conclusion by reading this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You say in your statement, regarding the PTT, that they weren't in use, but that you were using mobile communication facilities. Can you describe what those mobile communication facilities were and where they were located.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that we used them. I said that we had some of the assets, outdated equipment, that could be used as mobile communications. We had our own stationary communication system based on the switchboard and radio relay equipment. There was a unit there that was a battalion, but it only had the strength of a company. There were some 70 men and some 70 vehicles, which up until Bosansko Grahovo fell, and on the eve of the aggression, were in the northern barracks. Later on, they were relocated into the direction of Padjene, since the plan was that in the event of an aggression, the Main Staff was supposed to be relocated to Srb. That was a fallback population. Of course, the Main Staff being in Knin was in the close proximity of the front line. We had that unit -- mobile unit with some ten men and some ten vehicles which had communications equipment mounted on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to show you 65 ter 428, please. Mr. Novakovic, let me ask you, are you familiar with any individuals with the name either Medo or Zezelj?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear such names. Zezelj is a probably a family name, and Medo must be a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a telephone intercept of a conversation that General Mrksic had while he was in Knin. It's the 4 the of August, 1995, 2158 hours. He talks about what transpired during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go toward the bottom in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He says: "Well, it's finished here. Knin is being emptied, relocation is organised. "Then, well, can you go to the city? "Well, we will defend Knin tomorrow and the day after tomorrow in any way we can." Now, is that your understanding --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Then if we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Knin is empty, but we will defend." Now, that on the evening of the 4th was, in fact, the intent wasn't it, Mr. Novakovic? You had evacuated the civilians, but the military was still going to stay and defend the city of Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I mentioned a meeting held in the commander's office, and the commander issued tasks at 2030 to the commander of the Northern Dalmatia Corps and the commander of our brigade, not only to defend Knin but the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of page 2, he says: "Well, they didn't, it's just that they put the panic in Knin. "Well, panic schmanic. Prevent it, execute by rifles. "You can't do that. It's a stampede. No control there. Better that than for me to lose people. It's better that they get pulled out in an organised manner than that I lose them." The other person says: "Don't let the troops go." Now, what transpired on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Well, women and children can't drive cars, can they? Army has much more to do. There are people in Benkovac, and they didn't even start moving out yet." Now, you had a problem on the evening of the 4th because soldiers were starting to desert their positions as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained this. Individual soldiers would leave. I don't know if you can call it desertion. They would leave to see how their families fared. They were compelled to. There was shelling, and more of the shells landed across the front lines than on the front lines themselves. So the answer to your question might be a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to that issue, because a little bit towards the middle of that page, he says: "Well, F it. The communication assets in Knin are not working. They shot everything in this morning. I was left without electricity, TV, radio, everything, man." What they shot out on the morning of the 4th, Mr. Novakovic, was your communication abilities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, they fired upon the radio and television building. I think that the first shell that landed in Knin was the one that landed on the radio and television centre. As for the communications devices, in the course of the night, the communication system in the command was operational. The commanders who were out in the field were in touch with the command because the communication centre in the command was not completely destroyed. Parts of it were damaged, admittedly. The answer could be that they were, yes, targeted, but not solely the communications facility. The town itself was shelled in addition to or along with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D948, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D948 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, the last thing I asked you Friday was how much time you would need. You said "I expect to finish in the first session."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I will be closer to the ten hours I indicated before. If I could have another 45 minutes, just to go through the rest of the targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will consider it with my colleagues, and I let you know after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises again for the late start. There were good reasons for it, but I do understand that is not pleasant for the parties and for the witness who is waiting. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, at your most recent witness statement, which I believe is P1094, at paragraph 31, you say that: "The Tvik factory, to my knowledge, there was no military use made of this factory." I'd like to show you a report from TV Knin from September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this 1D61-0236. Can I proceed, Mr. President. May we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]. "Speaker: Despite the four years of war and the imposed embargo, the state owned company Tvik from Knin has been successfully resisting any hardship. The commander of the Serb army of the Krajina, Major-General Milan Celeketic, visited this company today along with his associates. "Reporter: As part of his regular activities of visiting commercial companies, the SVK commander, Major-General Milan Celeketic, accompanied by his logistics assistant, Major-General Mirko Bjelanovic, and Colonel Dusan Smiljanic, visited the this morning the state owned company, the screw tractor Tvik in Knin. While talking to the manager of this company, Mr. Jugoslav Pavlovic, the commander was informed about the difficulties Tvik has been faced with under conditions of war and the blockade of the international market. "At the time the war broke out, the Tvik factory had 3.300 employees. The number was reduced to 2.300 employees today, of which more than 1.000 are conscripts. Still, Tvik managed to fulfil any obligations towards the employees, the workers waiting to reassume their work place and the conscripts. 50 per cent of this company's production was designated for export, but today it offers the cheapest products on the Yugoslav market. "Mr. Pavlovic, the manager of Tvik, has assured the visitors that once the borders are reopened and export it possible again, this company could reassume regular business operations. General Celeketic and Mr. Pavlovic also discussed the military production programme in Tvik. After that, the commander and his associates visited the production facilities of this extremely important company."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In order to speed it up, Your Honour, I tender this video into evidence. I have will one more document, and then I will put some questions to the witness about the Tvik factory. So I tender the video into evidence right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D949, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D949 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have 1D61-0272, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. Novakovic, dated 10 July 1995. It's from the Ministry of Defence, and it says: "Due to the urgent need of constructing lethal devices to be launched from an earth bound rocket launcher and given the capacity the Tvik tractor, Knin, (tool factory), we have allocated part of the production of certain products in cooperation with the Banja metal factory, Dvorna Uni, to the aforementioned factory." Third paragraph: "I propose that the Tvik factory, Knin, (tool factory) be put into the work system of the sector for military and special purpose production at least for a certain period of time, and that the requirements of the sector for military and special purpose production be considered a work priority. "Deputy Minister, Colonel Milan Suput." Mr. Novakovic, this is from the 10th of July, 1995. Were you aware -- first, you saw, in the video, the military production programme. Can you help us understand what that programme was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Today Mr. Misetic is showing the date of the 10 July. The video we saw was September 1994, so that should be made clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. We have noted that. The evidence is for the Chamber to consider. Mr. Hedaraly, this is an inappropriate intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are asked about your awareness of this, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware of that. We didn't see the programme actually in the video. It was only mentioned. And by the way, I already said that during that period, I was not in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it apparently becomes an issue of time, because what is put to you in this document is July 1995, where a clear role is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was there during this particular period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in this period of time, apart from what we saw in the video, where, only in general terms, mention is made of a military programme, which at least suggests that there was a military programme. Here now we find a very specific assignment of a certain task in military production.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I visited this factory on several occasions, and I never noticed any military production. I know that all our factories before the war had certain programmes, but the question is whether they were able to implement them. If I may comment on the last passage in this information dated 10th of July, the deputy minister, Mr. Suput, only proposes that this factory be included in the system of special production programme, but he doesn't specifically say what it is all about. Also, we cannot see whether anything was done regarding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about whether you were aware of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said I visited the factory several times. I didn't see any production of that kind there. I know that there was maintenance detail in the -- in the factory, numbering some 300 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, nevertheless, I asked you whether you were aware of it. You said, "I went there. I didn't it, "which doesn't mean that you could not be aware by other sources, such as documents, discussions, or other information you received. Were you aware that Tvik was, among other matters perhaps, but was also active productive in military production? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't aware, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Since you weren't aware any military production at Tvik, Mr. Novakovic, where did the ammunition for the army of the RSK come from.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the ammunition came from the reserves of the JNA that had existed there. In Golubic, there were between 8 and 10.000 tons of ammunition, and these were the reserves of the military command and the military district. We also had access to the depot in Sveti Rok and in Cerkezovac. It is it possible that a smaller quantity of ammunition had come from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but I don't know the exact amounts, and whether that happened often or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could go back to D923, please -- I'm sorry. If I could tender 1D62-0272 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from Mr. Hedaraly, I see. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D950 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, again D923, please. If we could go to page 24 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again here on channel 4 a French translation of my words. So, apparently there was a small problem, but I think we can now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All the way to the bottom, please, so I can see the numbered page. 24, I'm sorry. I didn't speak clearly enough, and that's page 16 in the B/C/S. Yes. It's numbered paragraph 3. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now General Mrksic reports on 26th August, and he says: "Due to the incessant activity of the enemy artillery and rocket system, from the Senjak barracks in Knin, where at the very beginning of the attack, three trucks had been destroyed and a driver was killed, it was not possible to carry out any relocation of quarter master or any other material supplies." Were you aware, Mr. Novakovic, that at the beginning of the operation, that three trucks had been destroyed and a driver killed in the Senjak barracks?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two drivers were killed. There were the employees of the transport company Lika Trans. I'm not sure whether they were conscripts or civilians, but, any way, two of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about the trucks, were you aware that trucks were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These two men were driving those trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to turn your attention briefly to the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go, Mr. Registrar, to 1D61-0171, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I'm going to show you an intercepted telephone conversation between General Ratko Mladic and an unknown individual on the 6th of August at 0938.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go towards the bottom and it is towards the bottom in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, if we could go to the next page, please, I'm sorry. And if we could go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mladic says, and it's bold: "Well, in the north, things are good, but down south, it looks like they did something stupid. They wrote an evacuation order for women and children, and that caused a mass exodus. "They were holding positions all over successfully, at all the lines. The area around Crvena Zemlja towards Knin, it was a bit more under a threat; however, it was the police that abandoned those positions."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go down further in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says -- the unknown voice says: "Let me tell you, this guy is celebrating up in Zagreb. You've surely heard he needs to be shut up so that this is minimised." The unknown voice tells Mladic: "Now the rear depends on you. Yes, yes, put pressure on from that side. I will most likely be in contact with father tomorrow." Now, what is being discussed there, Mr. Novakovic, from a military perspective, is that someone is telling General Mladic to put pressure on General Gotovina's forces in Bosnia that are holding the line against the -- General Mladic's forces in Bosnia. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to comment on this. I was never involved in this kind of communications and exchanges. I was in charge of information which was public domain; therefore, I wouldn't be able to comment on this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you this: Based on the fact that you were someone who was a relatively high level individual in these circles at the time, when someone says, "Put pressure on from that side. I will most likely be in contact with father tomorrow," do you have any idea who "father" might be?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know even know -- or I don't know even know who these people involved in the conversation are, and, therefore, I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 1D61-0171 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D951, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D951 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to show just a very brief portion of a videotape, which I am bar table, but it is in response to the map produced by the witness on the front lines. I have tendered the underlying documents to the Prosecution. It is a video produced by the Defence. It is, Mr. Registrar, 1D61-0246. Your Honour, I am going to show you the legend of this map on Sanction because it may be a little bit difficult to read on the video. But what we've done is we've put in red the front line of the ARSK and ARS. The blue line is the front line of the HV and HVO. The green line is the front line of ABiH forces, as of the 3rd of August, and then three is a solid blue line. Then the border between Split Military District and Gospic is in black, which, our position, would be after Operation Storm. The brown line is the international border. Just so the Court is aware of what this is, these are the lines and it is a movie made of satellite imagery, so that you can see the precise points of the line, all the way up and down, of the terrain and topography. So I will just show the first few seconds of it, so just you're aware of what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
